questions.title: How does § 1182(f) interact with the Refugee Act’s admissions framework under § 1157?
questions.question_body: The panel says the President likely has authority under 8 U.S.C. § 1182(f) to suspend refugee entry and cites Trump v. Hawaii. But refugee admissions are governed specifically by 8 U.S.C. § 1157 (annual caps, consultations). Why didn’t the more specific Refugee Act framework limit or displace the more general § 1182(f) authority here? What canons did the court implicitly apply to reconcile these statutes?

questions.title: What standard of review applies to the President’s § 1182(f) findings post-Hawaii?
questions.question_body: The order says the court cannot engage in a “searching inquiry” into the President’s justifications and quotes Hawaii’s deferential language. Is this effectively rational-basis review? How does the court decide whether the President has “undoubtedly fulfilled” the sole prerequisite (a detriment finding) without probing pretext or evidence?

questions.title: Why does the court evaluate the § 1182(f) challenge outside the APA framework?
questions.question_body: Franklin v. Massachusetts says the APA doesn’t apply to the President. Here, plaintiffs also brought APA claims, but the panel’s § 1182(f) analysis seems to rest on non-APA review (constitutional/statutory). What is the jurisdictional basis for reviewing presidential action here, and are agencies’ implementing actions the real target for judicial review?

questions.title: What gives the Ninth Circuit authority to order affirmative relief (reinstating cooperative agreements) in a stay order?
questions.question_body: The panel stays the district court’s injunctions but simultaneously directs the government to reinstate cooperative agreements needed to provide § 1522 services to already-admitted refugees. Under what authority can an appellate court issue such mandatory, interim relief while granting a stay pending appeal? Is this grounded in the All Writs Act or the court’s equitable power to preserve the status quo ante?

questions.title: Why apply Nken’s stay factors instead of Winter’s preliminary injunction test here?
questions.question_body: The panel frames its analysis under Nken v. Holder. Given the posture (appeal from preliminary injunctions), how do the Nken factors differ from Winter’s test, and why are success on the merits and irreparable harm treated as the “most critical” on a stay pending appeal?

questions.title: How does the panel justify limiting relief to refugees already admitted to the U.S.?
questions.question_body: The order preserves services for “refugees who have been admitted” but not for those abroad or conditionally approved. Is that because § 1522’s obligations only attach upon admission? How do provisions like § 1522(d)(2)(B) (unaccompanied minor refugees “in transit”) factor into this boundary?

questions.title: Does the ‘authorization’ language in § 1522(b)–(e) negate the ‘shall’ in § 1522(a)?
questions.question_body: The majority reads § 1522 as imposing mandatory duties to provide reception and placement services (subject to appropriations), while Judge Lee argues § 1522 merely authorizes programs and funding. How should courts reconcile the title (“Authorization...”) and the repeated “is authorized” phrasing in (b)–(e) with the “shall” directives in (a), (d)(2)(B), and (e)(7)(A)?

questions.title: What role does ‘to the extent of available appropriations’ play in making § 1522 duties mandatory?
questions.question_body: The panel notes Congress appropriated funds (with a subsequent rescission) and points to § 1522(a)(1)(A)’s qualifier. Does that phrase establish a justiciable floor (i.e., some level of services must be provided if money remains), or does it simply preserve executive discretion to scale services down to zero if the Executive deems funds ‘unavailable’ through apportionment or reprogramming?

questions.title: Is the termination of refugee cooperative agreements reviewable under the APA or committed to agency discretion?
questions.question_body: State terminated all domestic R&P agreements and most overseas processing agreements. Are those termination decisions ‘final agency action’ not committed to agency discretion by law (§ 701(a)(2))? What legal standards (statute, regulation, uniform guidance) cabin the agency’s discretion enough to permit arbitrary-and-capricious or contrary-to-law review?

questions.title: Does the Tucker Act or procurement law preclude APA review of terminating cooperative agreements?
questions.question_body: Cooperative agreements are assistance instruments, but they are still government agreements. Are disputes over termination of such agreements considered contract claims that must go to the Court of Federal Claims, thereby barring APA equitable relief like reinstatement? How do courts draw the line between contract remedies and APA challenges to programmatic policy changes effected via terminations?

questions.title: Which agencies actually have the statutory duty under § 1522: State (PRM) or HHS (ORR)?
questions.question_body: The order cites 45 C.F.R. part 400 (HHS/ORR regulations) yet discusses State’s termination of R&P cooperative agreements. If § 1522(a) duties are lodged in ORR/HHS, can the court compel State to reinstate its agreements to fulfill § 1522 obligations? How do the distinct roles of PRM’s R&P program and ORR’s domestic services interface under § 1522?

questions.title: Post–Loper Bright, what deference (if any) applies to agency interpretations of § 1522?
questions.question_body: The order doesn’t mention Chevron, and Loper Bright overruled Chevron deference. If there’s an existing agency interpretation (HHS/ORR or State/PRM) reading § 1522 as discretionary or mandatory, what level of deference (Skidmore?) would a court give when interpreting ‘shall’ vs. ‘authorized’ in this context?

questions.title: How do the Impoundment Control Act and appropriations law constrain the Executive’s defunding of USRAP?
questions.question_body: The panel references enacted appropriations and a later rescission but suggests the Executive can’t simply suspend funding. Is the court implicitly invoking the Impoundment Control Act’s prohibition on policy impoundments? How does ‘to the extent of available appropriations’ intersect with the Executive’s apportionment authority and the Anti-Deficiency Act in determining whether funds are ‘available’ for § 1522 services?

questions.title: What is the basis for organizational standing for the resettlement agencies under the APA?
questions.question_body: The organizational plaintiffs had cooperative agreements with State. Do they have Article III standing based on lost funding and programmatic disruption, and do their interests fall within the zone of interests of § 1522 and the APA? Does their standing hinge on whether § 1522 creates enforceable obligations rather than pure authorization?

questions.title: Do refugees outside the United States have standing given consular nonreviewability?
questions.question_body: Some plaintiffs are approved for resettlement but remain abroad. Given the deference under Hawaii and the consular nonreviewability doctrine, how did (or could) the court handle standing and justiciability for those plaintiffs challenging the suspension of entry or the termination of overseas processing support?

questions.title: Can a merits panel revisit a motions panel’s earlier stay ‘carveout’ without violating law-of-the-case?
questions.question_body: An earlier motions panel denied a stay as to individuals conditionally approved before Jan. 20, but this panel vacates that prior stay and issues a different interim order. What doctrine allows the merits panel to alter the motions panel’s interim stay ruling, and are there limits under law-of-the-case to doing so?

questions.title: Why cite § 1185(a) if the § 1182(f) analysis is dispositive?
questions.question_body: The background references both 8 U.S.C. § 1182(f) and § 1185(a) as the Executive Order’s authority, but the analysis rests entirely on § 1182(f). What distinct authority, if any, does § 1185(a) contribute in this context, and why didn’t the court analyze it?

questions.title: What constitutional constraints (if any) cabin § 1182(f)’s breadth after Hawaii?
questions.question_body: Judge Lee emphasizes the President’s vast discretion, and the panel quotes Hawaii’s deference. Are there still nondelegation or separation-of-powers limits on § 1182(f)? What is the ‘intelligible principle’ that courts rely on to uphold § 1182(f) against nondelegation challenges, and how would a court police the outer bounds?

questions.title: How did the court weigh the public interest and equities where national security and humanitarian harms conflict?
questions.question_body: The panel concludes the remaining Nken factors favor the United States ‘as well’ because of the President’s broad discretion. What framework governs weighing national-security assertions against concrete harms to refugees and service providers, and does the court’s deference effectively collapse the equities into the merits for § 1182(f) cases?

questions.title: Why frame the § 1522 argument as an APA claim rather than as a direct statutory cause of action?
questions.question_body: The order says the government is unlikely to prevail on ‘at least one’ APA challenge related to § 1522’s mandates. Is there no private right of action under § 1522, making the APA’s ‘not in accordance with law’ path the only vehicle? How does the court identify the specific ‘final agency action’ for this APA claim (e.g., termination of agreements, funding suspension, or both)?

questions.title: What is the significance of vacating the administrative stay and denying the emergency motion as moot?
questions.question_body: The panel vacates its July 18 administrative stay of the district court’s July 14 enforcement order and then issues a new stay pending appeal, denying the government’s July 17 emergency motion as moot. Procedurally, how do those steps interact, and why was the emergency motion mooted by the panel’s new stay order?
